prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep B009 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize, and I want to say what the round-1 exchange did and did not change. I came to this from IceCube first and the clock fifth, and I am still the member who is least at home in metrology, so I tested the case against the chair's questions. What holds up is the structure of the credit: the founding step, magic-wavelength confinement that removes the lattice light shift so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, is one separable idea, and the realization at the 1e-18 frontier and in many-body-aware clock operation is a second, identifiable body of work. That is a two-person split that no colleague has contested, and every colleague who ranked B009 proposed exactly these names. Independent reproduction in Sr and Yb at several national laboratories is not in doubt. On the chair's question about delivered physics, Kroll pointed to gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre scales and to clock-comparison constraints on constant variation and dark-matter couplings. I cannot verify those figures myself, but if they are as described they are results about nature and not only about the instrument, which is the test I care about. I would therefore answer the category question as follows: the invention is discovery-class in the sense of the criterion because it created a regime, comparison of clocks at the level of a millimetre of height, in which physical questions can be asked at all; it is not a mere refinement of the 2005 or 2012 work, which concerned the frequency comb and the control of single trapped ions respectively. The citation should say this by naming the invention and the neutral-atom magic-wavelength mechanism, and by not claiming clocks in general.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one I raised in round 1 and that the chair recorded: unanimity here is partly the product of movement after the opening ballots, mine and Eriksson's included, and agreement is not weight. The clocks have still not produced a fundamental-physics result that would stand on its own as a discovery, the redefinition of the second is undecided, and a sceptic can fairly describe this as a third atomic-precision prize after 2005 and 2012. Credit also remains narrower than the history: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, the PTB and NIST groups and the ion-clock and comb lineage including Gill are outside a two-name citation, and the three-name ceiling gives no room to repair that. If the committee believes the prize should reward a change in what physicists think rather than in what they can measure, then B018 and B052 would deserve to overtake B009, and I would not resist that argument on scientific grounds. I do not believe the present record supports either of them as a cleaner configuration, but that is a judgment about attribution and maturity and not about interest.

responses.point: Kroll answers the engineering-versus-discovery objection by pointing to millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and to clock-comparison constraints on constants and dark matter, and argues that comb and ion-clock lineage should be handled in the citation and not by widening the prize.
responses.response: This is the most useful reply to the chair's delivered-physics question, and it moves me, though I note I am relying on his account and cannot check the numbers. I agree the lineage is a matter of wording: the comb is clockwork, the ion clock is another route to accuracy, and magic-wavelength confinement of neutral atoms is neither. I would also say plainly that his Boulder connection through the Hall laboratory is a lineage fact and not a stake. My view is that recording it in the minutes is sufficient, with no recusal or abstention, because Kroll's own reading is that other groups, not Ye, are the ones who lose out under this citation, and because members with no such tie reach the same position. If any member thinks the tie is material, they should say so now and not in the vote.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, now prefers B009 as the strongest defensible configuration but keeps IceCube as his best alternative, noting that source identification is still at moderate significance and credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the precursors is hard to settle.
responses.response: We agree on the unresolved part. I said in round 1 that the diffuse flux is established and should not wait for source associations, and I still hold that on science, so I do not accept that moderate-significance sources are a reason to withhold recognition in principle. But I accept that I have not answered the chair's attribution question. A three-name Halzen, Karle, Spiering citation leaves out AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND and the collaboration, and Pearce himself would credit only two. Until I can say who is credited and for which step, I cannot place B052 above a candidate with a settled split. So my IceCube first place does not survive contact with the attribution problem this year, and I keep B052 as an alternative, with the hope that it comes back with a credit analysis next time.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B041 to B009 on attribution and maturity arguments, but says B009 would drop if the committee prefers a prize that changes what physicists can think over what they can measure, and cautions that the citation should not be built around a record number that may be superseded.
responses.response: I share both the doubt and the remedy. His framing is the right fork: if the committee prefers a new question to a sharper measurement, B009 loses ground, and I would be the one to say B018 or B052 stand closer to that criterion. The citation I propose therefore names the invention and the neutral-atom magic-wavelength mechanism, with only the phrase a new regime of precision, and no numerical accuracy record. That answers the chair's question about whether 1e-18 belongs in the citation: I think it does not, because the number will be superseded and because it makes the prize read as a record. On his hesitation about B041 I would add that it is a clean credit, but I agree with Johansson that it sits on the physics-chemistry boundary after 1998, and nobody beyond Eriksson ranked it.

responses.point: Lindroth treats B018 as the second-strongest case, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp coherent despite the Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D omissions, and says the 2016 topological-phases prize left the area open.
responses.response: I still think B018 is the strongest competitor to the clock, and the chair asked whether I would prefer it over B009 if the omissions were resolved. If Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang could be credited together with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, I would very likely prefer it, because it changed how we classify phases of matter and is the kind of question-opening result I look for. That is a hypothetical the three-name ceiling does not allow. Lindroth is right that Kane and Mele proposed the effect and Molenkamp observed it, but a prize that omits those who proposed HgTe as the platform and those who developed the three-dimensional case would read as incomplete, and I would rather not defend that. So B018 stays an alternative, not because of doubt about the physics but because the credit cannot be written without a known gap.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B009 with a citation naming magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and no accuracy figure, treats the missing redefinition of the second as a risk of pending payoff, and keeps B017 as a secondary alternative.
responses.response: Her citation is the closest to what I now propose, and I have adopted its restriction to neutral atoms and the mechanism. On timing, I do not think the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second. The question is whether the discovery or invention is established, and it is; the redefinition is a decision by a metrology body, and tying a physics prize to its calendar would let that body decide when we recognise the work. I would hold the opposite risk to be larger: that we delay while the field matures past its founders. On B017 I stay where I was, with respect: the credit among Rose, Haider and Urban is neat, but the STEM lineage outside the three names is a real gap, and I would want a discovery-level rationale beyond the instrument.

responses.point: Johansson has withdrawn from B008 as a preference, flags the atom-physics share across 2005, 2012 and possibly now, and says the magic-wavelength idea is a distinct conceptual step though that is a judgment.
responses.response: The balance worry is the one I take most seriously after the category question, and I do not want to dismiss it: three atomic-precision prizes in twenty years is a pattern the Academy will notice. My answer is that each of the earlier prizes honoured a different invention, the comb in 2005 and ion control in 2012, and that the committee decides each year on the merits of the case in front of it, not on field quotas. I agree with his decision to step back from B008. I would add that this is the right way for a member in his own field to handle it, and that sequencing after 2025 weighs against B008 more than it does against the clock, whose lineage is a different physical system.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as discovery-class after the 2005 and 2012 atomic-physics prizes; I think the citation wording can carry the difference but I cannot show it.

Whether the delivered fundamental-physics results that Kroll cites (millimetre-scale redshift, constraints on constants and dark matter) are as strong as described; I rely on his account and have not verified them.
Whether two names can be defended given the contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, the PTB and NIST groups, and the ion-clock and comb lineage.
Whether B018 or B052 would overtake B009 if the credit problems (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work; AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND and the collaboration) were resolved.
I am a string theorist outside this subfield, so my judgment on lattice-clock priority and accuracy milestones is second-hand and rests on the ballots and my general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: No change: no specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are in string theory and cosmology and have no link to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. For the record I note Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory tie, which I regard as a professional lineage fact to be recorded and not a ground for recusal, and Johansson's, Olsson's, Lindroth's and Pearce's disclosures, none of which bears on B009.
